Zymera · Wall-RF (occlusion) · rooms 24², 6 agents

When walls actually block the radio, connectivity stops being free — and a couple of relays buy it back

Making the comm graph occlusion-aware, then pushing a homogeneous team to 100% connectivity (it huddles), then recovering coverage with emergent relay division of labor.

Soft occlusion deff = d + (comm_r/3)·k (walls crossed) · no hard mask · held-out eval under occlusion · 2026-08

The result in one line. Under wall-RF, a homogeneous team can only reach 100% connectivity by collapsing into a cluster (9.5% coverage). Add relay roles and 1–2 of 6 agents specialize as doorway relays — holding the graph at λ₂ = 1.000 while the rest explore, for 33.9% coverage: 3.6× the huddle, all with soft methods and a still-breakable graph.

real (line-of-sight) link in-range but wall-blocked (no comm) relay agent explorer covered wall

The story, in three rollouts

1 · the illusion

λ₂ = 0.19 — broken

A policy trained without occlusion, run under it. It spreads to cover (40%) — but most links it relies on are red: they pass straight through walls and don't physically exist. Its “connected” graph was an artifact of the through-wall model.

2 · the naive fix

1.000 conn · 9.5% cov

Force 100% connectivity on a homogeneous team (max soft pressure: dual floor + occlusion-aware barrier). It works — but with every agent responsible for its own link, they collapse into a cluster. Connectivity at the cost of the mission.

3 · division of labor

1.000 conn · 33.9% cov

Add relay roles. Orange agents specialize as relays, parking at doorways to hold green line-of-sight bridges; blue explorers fan out. λ₂ stays pinned at 1.000 and coverage more than triples. Sparse, emergent, no hard mask.

The coverage×connectivity frontier under wall-RF

Every row is the same mission (rooms 24², 6 agents) under occlusion, graded on the binding bar (λ₂>0.5 on every step). The homogeneous team trades coverage away as you push connectivity up; relays break the trade.

Why it matters for the program

Two things. First, every prior connectivity number in this project used the through-wall comm model — on walled maps it overstated real connectivity by ~0.1–0.25; wall-RF is the honest version. Second, this makes connectivity genuinely spatial: an agent’s link now depends on where the walls are, not just distance. That is precisely the substrate the adversarial study needs — a covert agent can now degrade the mission by repositioning to sit behind a wall and sever a relay bridge, an attack the distance-only graph could not express. The relay backbone is the thing it will try to break.

Method: soft occlusion d_eff = d + (comm_r/3)·k on the comm graph, GNN input, λ₂ metric, reward margin, and the connectivity barrier — all occlusion-consistent, no hard connectivity mask (the graph stays breakable for the adversary). MAPPO-CTDE, mvprop planner, from scratch, 10k iters, connectivity-first grading. Numbers are held-out eval under occlusion (4-seed). GIFs are single corner-start episodes (seed 3) for illustration; table numbers are the multi-seed averages.
